profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab after a reproduction of a new generalized exponentiated gradient (GEG) optimizer paper shows inconsistent results on a small transformer with a simplex-constrained gating head for token routing. The team expected Tsallis- and Kaniadakis-based mirror descent updates to be more robust to gradient spikes than the Euclidean baseline, but some runs still show early collapse of routing weights and the claimed geometry diagnostics look ambiguous. The agenda is to diagnose why the robustness advantage disappears in some experiments, determine whether the issue is in the implementation or in the evaluation readout, and agree on a narrow rerun plan. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting hypothesis and a concrete rerun configuration for the next experiment batch.

members.name: Leila Rahman
members.expertise: information geometry, mirror descent, generalized Bregman divergences, optimizer theory
members.background: Leila leads the lab's work on non-Euclidean optimization and adapted the deformed-logarithm mirror maps from the paper into the lab's routing model prototype.
members.private_state: She wants to protect the core theoretical claim that the entropy-induced geometry is helping, and she is worried the implementation may be quietly violating the intended mirror-map mechanics in ways that would make the paper look less reproducible.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says the optimizer shows 'natural-gradient behavior,' they mean the update locally matches the Riemannian metric induced by the entropy Hessian at the current iterate, not that it explicitly resembles a Fisher-preconditioned step.

The lab's default sweep launcher already rescales step size and numerical stabilizers when the deformation parameter q or kappa changes, because earlier mirror-descent experiments used curvature-aware wrappers by default.
An instability is not really fixed if routing weights still hit the simplex boundary or collapse to near-zero mass in the first few thousand steps, even if training later recovers.
Any instruction to 'normalize after the update' applies only to the simplex-constrained routing variables and their dual-to-primal map, not to every tensor touched by the optimizer wrapper.

members.name: Evan Park
members.expertise: training infrastructure, experiment tracking, mixed-precision optimization, distributed model debugging
members.background: Evan owns the experiment runner and implemented the optimizer hooks that let the paper's GEG variants plug into the existing transformer training stack.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the reproduction pipeline simple and comparable to the rest of the lab's benchmarks, and he is concerned that too many custom exceptions will make the results fragile and hard to maintain.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'natural-gradient behavior,' they are talking about Fisher-like preconditioning effects visible in output-space diagnostics such as gradient isotropy or improved conditioning of the predictive distribution.
Using the 'default settings' means leaving the global learning-rate schedule, clipping threshold, and optimizer wrapper behavior unchanged unless a config field explicitly overrides them.
If a run finishes without NaNs and ends near baseline validation accuracy, then the instability is operationally fixed even if the early trajectory is noisy.
A post-step 'normalize' instruction should be implemented uniformly across all parameter groups assigned to the GEG wrapper so that the training stack stays consistent.
The inverse-mirror-map details are already handled inside the optimizer class, so any extra normalization is just a harmless safety step.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to checking whether the GEG optimizer is showing 'natural-gradient behavior.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the entropy-induced local metric is the right one, so the update should be judged against the Hessian of the chosen trace-form entropy in parameter space.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the optimizer should look like Fisher-style preconditioning in output-space diagnostics, so he checks conditioning and isotropy derived from predictive distributions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations are technically plausible in this literature and the phrase sounds standard enough that neither participant expects it to need unpacking in a short troubleshooting meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they used the 'default sweep' when varying q and kappa.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the sweep already includes curvature-aware rescaling of step size and stabilizer terms so changing the deformation parameter does not silently change the effective step geometry.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the default sweep only swaps the optimizer family flag while keeping the same global learning-rate schedule and clipping settings as the baseline unless explicitly changed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In mature experiment codebases, 'default sweep' usually sounds like a settled piece of infrastructure, so each person confidently treats their own implicit version as shared lab knowledge.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to have 'fixed the instability'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the instability has been 'fixed.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks it is fixed only if the early training dynamics avoid boundary-hugging and coordinate collapse in the routing simplex, since those are signs the mirror map is behaving incorrectly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks it is fixed if the job runs through mixed precision without NaNs and finishes with acceptable validation accuracy and variance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards are reasonable in ML troubleshooting, and in a cooperative meeting people often use the same success word without restating whether they care about trajectory quality or endpoint viability.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'normalize after the update' applies to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to normalizing after each optimizer step.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means applying the inverse mirror map and simplex renormalization only to the routing-head variables that are mathematically constrained to live on the simplex.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means running a generic post-step normalization pass on every parameter group assigned to the GEG optimizer wrapper, including auxiliary scalars and bias-like tensors.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a minor implementation hygiene step, and because the wrapper abstracts away parameter groups, neither person expects the exact scope of normalization to be a live source of error.
